Fox examines the challenges and limitations facing the Big Bang theory, emphasizing both how it withstands scrutiny and the aspects of the universe it does not fully explain as of 2002. [19] [2] The author explores classic cosmological problems that had confronted the standard Big Bang model, including the horizon problem (why distant regions of the universe appear so uniform despite being causally disconnected), the flatness problem (why the universe's density is so precisely balanced near the critical value), the homogeneity problem (why the universe is smooth on large scales), and the magnetic monopole problem (why predicted relics from grand unified theories are not observed). [9] Fox discusses how these issues prompted the addition of cosmic inflation to the model, an extension not originally part of the Big Bang framework but necessary to account for the observed large-scale structure and uniformity rather than a merely homogeneous mix of light elements. [15] Evidence and why the theory works The book outlines three primary lines of observational evidence that underpin the Big Bang theory and account for its status as the dominant cosmological model. [18] Fox emphasizes the expansion of the universe, first inferred from Edwin Hubble's observations of galactic redshifts, which show that distant galaxies are receding from us at speeds proportional to their distance, indicating that space itself is stretching over time. [9] This expansion implies that the universe was denser and hotter in the past, aligning with a hot origin rather than a static or alternative framework. [9] Another cornerstone presented is the cosmic microwave background radiation, discovered in 1965 as a faint, uniform glow permeating space at a temperature of about 2.7 K. [9] The book describes this radiation as the relic thermal emission from when the universe cooled enough for atoms to form, roughly 380,000 years after the Big Bang, with its near-perfect blackbody spectrum and small fluctuations providing direct evidence of the early hot phase. [9] Measurements available by 2002, including those from the COBE satellite, confirmed its properties and supported the theory's predictions with high precision. [9] Fox
